subtype_info: Talaromyces marneffei infection in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus
title: Talaromyces marneffei Infection in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Patients: Report of Two Cases and Review of the Literature
case_text:
A 49-year-old Chinese man, who had a 2-month history of SLE and treated with oral prednisone (30 mg/day), was admitted to a local hospital in February 2017 due to repeated fever, cough and fatigue. He was a farmer living in Guangxi. During hospitalization, Gram-negative bacteria were isolated from his blood culture and antibiotic (meropenem) for septicemia administered during a period of 3 weeks without improvement. He was then referred to our hospital for further treatment.
Upon admission to our hospital, physical examination showed annular erythema of the inner canthus and eyelids, a mouth ulcer and massive ecchymosis of the forearms. Routine blood examination revealed the following: white blood cells, 3.65 x 109/L with 81.4% neutrophils; hemoglobin, 85.80 g/L; and platelets, 649.20 x 109/L. The c-reactive protein (CRP) level (38.99 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (>140 mm/hour) were elevated. The 24-hour urine protein level was 2655.0 mg, anti-dsDNA antibody titers were normal, and serum complements were low (C3, 0.519 g/l; C4, 0.125 g/l). Assessment for anti-nuclear antibody and anti-SS-A indicated positivity while anti-HIV antibody was not detected. The liver functions (alanine aminotransferase, 144 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase 677 U/L) were deranged, and blood coagulation (thrombin time >120 s, fibrinogen 0.69 g/l) was impaired. The CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (95 cells/microL) was lower than normal. A sputum smear contained hyphae. Chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed infiltration in the upper lobes of the lungs, swollen mediastinal lymph nodes, and a slight pleural effusion. A diagnosis of active SLE with lupus nephritis, pneumonia, and septicemia was established.
He received intravenous methylprednisolone (80 mg/day), empirical intravenous antibacterial (meropenem 1gq8h), and antifungal (fluconazole 200 mg/day). His temperature subsequently returned to normal. However, his platelet count progressively declined to 42.4 x 109/L and he developed hemoptysis. Nine days post-admission, chest CT showed increased infiltration and pleural effusion. Finally, the sputum and bone marrow cultures were positive for T. marneffei.
Methylprednisolone was changed to prednisone 50 mg/day. Intravenous amphotericin B (5 mg/day gradually increased to 25 mg/day) and oral voriconazole (400 mg/day) were administered for 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole (400 mg/day) for 11 months. His condition improved and there was no recurrence of T. marneffei infection at the 3-year follow-up.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Talaromycosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Talaromyces marneffei infection in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus
